title: Toward a novel framework of understanding the relationship between social media use and political knowledge: a systematic literature review
authors: Cato Waeterloos, Desiree Schmuck, Peter Van Aelst, Michaël Opgenhaffen
abstract: While recent quantitative research finds little evidence that citizens learn about politics from social media, it is unclear whether studies adequately capture platform complexity and often fragmented understandings of political knowledge. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically reviewed 78 papers that assess the quantitative association between social media use and political knowledge. Our critical assessment of how such studies conceptualize and operationalize social media use and political knowledge revealed a dual mismatch. First, social media use is often measured via general frequency, overlooking specific content (beyond “news”), actors (e.g., influencers), platforms (beyond Facebook/Twitter), and exposure modes (e.g., incidental). Second, knowledge measures remain conservative, focusing on institutional facts while neglecting issue-specific and noninstitutional topics. We propose a novel 3-dimensional framework and methodological pathways to address key limitations in the dominant normative tradition of studying the relationship between social media and political learning.
journal_full: Annals of the International Communication Association

title: Post hoc illusion—how the knew-it-all-along effect undermines trust
authors: Drew B Margolin, Mariken van der Velden
abstract: This article introduces a theory of distrust called the post hoc illusion. The post hoc illusion is a mistaken belief about what others knew in the past. It arises when stakeholders, who have entrusted power to the deciders, infer that the decider “overlooked” facts that were “obvious” and should have been consulted. We show how this effect is a logical consequence of constraints in human abductive processes–the manner in which human minds create and evaluate causal explanations. A research agenda for the post hoc illusion is then proposed, beginning with the identification of key variables that should influence its operation: relevant facts present in the past and theoretical novelty. We then argue that the illusion can be ameliorated through narratives that portray the decider’s state of mind in the past.

title: Digital Agency Tools: A Way to Buffer the Negative Effects of Excessive Phone Use?
authors: Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay
abstract: In times of ubiquitous smartphone use, most users adopt one or more self-imposed rules regarding their device usage, also known as voluntary digital disconnection. Drawing on the Integrative Model of Mobile Media Use and Need Experiences (IM³UNE), this study provides empirical evidence on the adoption of digital agency tools and their potential in mitigating ill-being (depression, anxiety, and stress) associated with excessive smartphone use. We conducted a quota-based online survey involving n = 384 ( M age = 49.6) smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium). The results provide a systematization of different digital agency tools, showing they are widely used among adults. Importantly, we provide preliminary evidence on their potential in buffering ill-being due to excessive smartphone use. For users of detox apps and in-app well-being features, the associations between excessive use and ill-being were nonsignificant, unlike for nonusers of these tools. For users of default device settings, such as iOS ScreenTime, there were no differences. Our findings contribute to theory by applying and empirically testing critical elements of the IM³UNE model. Empirically, our findings indicate the importance of studying different types of tools, as they do not appear to be equally beneficial.

title: Weekly Gaming Duration and Internet Gaming Disorder in Relation to Depression and Loneliness: A Two-Year Follow-Up Study
authors: Joshua J. Condry, Isabel C. Singer, Zachary A. Reese
abstract: The current study examined the association between weekly video game engagement and mental health, specifically Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD), loneliness, and depression. We recruited 377 U.S. adults through CloudResearch Connect using gaming-frequency quotas, resulting in a sample representing a wide range of weekly gaming duration (range = 0–80 hours, M = 14.62). Analyses revealed that weekly gameplay hours did not consistently predict depression and loneliness. In contrast, people with higher IGD scores tended to have higher weekly playtime, more depressive symptoms, and greater feelings of loneliness. We readministered the same survey 2 years later ( N = 172 or 45.6 percent of baseline sample). Here, we found that both higher weekly hours and higher IGD scores at baseline predicted increases in depressive symptoms 2 years later, controlling for their baseline depression. We did not find that gaming was predictive of loneliness longitudinally. These findings are particularly relevant given the American Psychiatric Association’s interest in IGD in the DSM-5 coupled with the ongoing public debate about the benefits and ills of video games. Our findings suggest that people who struggle to balance gaming with other life demands may experience more depressive symptoms over time. Thus, clinicians may opt to focus on helping clients with IGD better balance their priorities.

title: How AI agents’ self-disclosure in initial interactions shapes user perceptions: evidence from dual cognitive pathways
authors: Minqian Yang, Pei-Luen Patrick Rau
abstract: Purpose As users increasingly engage with various unfamiliar artificial intelligence (AI) agents, initial impressions become crucial. AI agents’ self-disclosure can play a key role in shaping these impressions. This study aims to conceptualize AI agents’ self-disclosure, identify key user perceptual factors and examine how self-disclosure influences user perceptions through different cognitive pathways. Design/methodology/approach A two-stage questionnaire survey was conducted. Firstly, exploratory factor analysis was employed to identify key perceptual factors shaped by AI self-disclosure and to examine their effects on users’ willingness to use. Then, users’ willingness to use the AI agents adopting different self-disclosure styles across utilitarian and hedonic scenarios was investigated, and the underlying cognitive mechanisms were further analyzed. Findings Three core perceptual factors were identified: perceived social individuality, perceived reliability and perceived emotional support. In both utilitarian and hedonic scenarios, users consistently preferred an emotional (over factual) tone for relation-oriented self-disclosure, which incorporated richer social cues, and a detailed (over brief) style for transparency-oriented self-disclosure, which conveyed more machine-related characteristics. Perceived social individuality was found to play a more important role in users’ evaluation of AI agents’ relation-oriented self-disclosure. The results provide empirical support for a dual perspective of AI agents that can be shaped by self-disclosure: relation-oriented self-disclosure activates social responses, whereas transparency-oriented self-disclosure triggers machine-based evaluations. Originality/value This study proposes and empirically validates the concept of AI self-disclosure as a dual-dimensional construct. By uncovering the mechanisms through which it shapes initial perceptions, it offers actionable insights for designing more transparent and socially attuned AI agents.

title: What factors build user trust in human–technology relationships? An exploratory meta-analysis of the key antecedents to trust in IT artifacts
authors: Thuy Duong Oesterreich, Eduard Anton, Matthias Söllner, Frank Teuteberg
abstract: Purpose In response to various calls for more research extending our understanding of trust in IT artifacts, we synthesize the empirical evidence of prior studies in the rich stream of trust-related research to gain a more consistent picture regarding the role of trust antecedents in human–technology relationships. Design/methodology/approach We conduct an exploratory meta-analysis of 374 primary studies reported in 348 articles covering 26 years of trust research to gain deeper insights into the role of the antecedents to trust in IT artifacts. Our research framework combines 19 independent variables conceptualizing human- and system-like trusting beliefs, technology acceptance factors, system characteristics, user characteristics and contextual factors with perceived risk, trusting intention and trusting behavior as the dependent variables. Findings The findings confirm the pervasive role of the human- and system-like trusting beliefs ability/competence, benevolence, reliability and helpfulness as well as the technology acceptance factors perceived enjoyment and perceived usefulness in building trust and fostering trusting behavior. In addition, the findings indicate the importance of the system characteristics security and privacy in forming trust and helping users overcome the perceived degree of uncertainty on the way to fostering behavioral and continuous intention. Originality/value Based on the findings, we discuss the implications for research and practice, propose design recommendations for increasing trust in IT artifacts and provide future research avenues to explore. Considering that trust significantly influences IT adoption, our study's integrated perspective on trust is crucial for deepening our understanding of key factors in fostering trust between humans and technology.

title: Assimilating generative AI into ideation work: seeding, search and human contribution
authors: Jafar Sabbah, Aneesh Banerjee, Feng Li
abstract: Purpose This paper examines how generative AI (GenAI) systems can be assimilated into idea generation (ideation) work so that human–GenAI collaboration augments creativity. It asks which seeding configurations with GenAI improve novelty, utility and feasibility, and examines preliminary process evidence regarding human contribution to joint search. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a search-based view of creativity, we conceptualise GenAI as an information system that structures individuals' search and evaluation of information. We test four configurations with 400 professionals: human-only ideation, unstructured human–GenAI collaboration, GenAI seeding and a TC-based GenAI configuration. Expert evaluators rate novelty, utility and feasibility. Findings Statistically reliable improvements in novelty, utility, or feasibility were not detected for either unstructured human–GenAI collaboration or conventional GenAI seeding. The TC-based GenAI configuration, by contrast, significantly improves novelty relative to unstructured collaboration and conventional seeding. Statistically significant differences in utility were not detected relative to either GenAI comparison condition, while feasibility was lower relative to conventional seeding. Practical implications Organisations should not assume that simply enabling GenAI in ideation tools will improve creative outcomes. When seeking to promote novelty, organisations may consider the full TC-based GenAI configuration tested here, combining a short TC orientation with TC-based GenAI-generated seeds. Originality/value The study advances information systems research on AI assimilation and human–AI collaboration by showing that creative augmentation is not automatic and depends on how GenAI is configured to structure joint search. It identifies the TC-based GenAI configuration as a concrete way to enhance novelty in human–GenAI ideation.

title: Rejection of cross-cutting news depends on content, sources, and cultural contexts: evidence from online trace data
authors: Wonjeong Jo, Magdalena Wojcieszak
abstract: We examine the conditions in which people reject cross-cutting news in naturalistic settings of online comments. Theoretically, we account for article content and source to test whether commenters’ rejection and its intensity depend on whether cross-cutting news (a) is hostile to their in-group or favorable to the out-group and (b) is “unexpected” (from in-group sources) or “expected” (from out-group sources). Methodologically, we use online traces from news aggregators in South Korea (SK; 7,607 comments) and the United States (116,308 comments). We find that most commenters (79% in SK and 64% in the United States) reject cross-cutting news, with left-leaning commenters expressing stronger rejection than right-leaning commenters. Regarding article content, the SK commenters more strongly rejected in-group hostility, while the U.S. commenters rejected out-group favoritism more. Regarding article source, SK commenters more strongly rejected unexpected cross-cutting news from in-group sources than expected cross-cutting news from out-group sources. We discuss the implications of these findings.

title: Writing the Situated Self: Intersectional and Geographic Patterning in College Admissions Essays
authors: AJ Alvero, anthony lising antonio, Leslie Luqueño, Francis Pearman
abstract: Written language is often considered a reflection of the author's internal thoughts, states, and characteristics. This is why writing is used in evaluation to make inferences about authors, but also why social scientists use text as a lens into psychological states. We present a complementary perspective: that writing systematically reflects the social environments of authors. We explore these dynamics in a large corpus of college admissions essays ( n = 232,838 essays submitted by 76,510 self-identified Hispanic applicants from 2015 to 2017) and metadata about author sociodemographics, including the ZIP code of their high school, gender identity, and household income. We find that intersectional demographic markers are highly salient. We further demonstrate that ZIP code-level socioeconomic measures are strongly correlated with the writing style and content of local applicants. Finally, we show that misclassification rates vary geographically and are modestly associated with local demographic composition and social capital, indicating that writing is influenced both socially and geographically. By documenting strong alignment between text and authors that is observable through machine reading, our findings clarify how author demographics and context structure what is written and, stylistically, how. Framing text as an external, social process rather than purely internal creates opportunities to bridge psychological and sociological data, methods, and theories to better understand the connections between language and society, especially in moments of evaluation. Because these texts were produced before the popularization of large language models (LLMs), our results serve as useful benchmarks for archival work and also generate new questions as LLMs mediate written self-presentation.
journal_full: Journal of Language and Social Psychology

title: The Making of Media Entertainment
authors: Robert Joel Lewis
abstract: Abstract: Entertainment science remains a mosaic of disconnected research streams, each generating valuable insights but lacking a cross-cutting mechanism to reveal their connections. Existing understandings do not link different areas of theory, such as research on entertainment’s appeal versus research on its maladaptive effects. This paper proposes that attending to how entertainment is made can bridge these streams. What entertainment is, on this view, is a technology: entertainment is a deliberately iterated system of superstimuli (unnaturally attention-grabbing stimuli that activate evolved cognitive mechanisms) that producers refine to capture audiences and serve their own goals. Drawing on predictive-mind frameworks from computational neuroscience, this paper treats attention as precision-weighted Bayesian inference and shows how entertainment taps that inference architecture using increasingly sophisticated superstimulus technologies. This view reveals attention capture as a common principle underlying diverse entertainment phenomena. It (a) provides a principled taxonomy that maps research domains onto the evolved mechanisms content activates, (b) reframes and resolves the paradox of suspense, (c) generates first-principles predictions about content evolution and cultivation effects, and (d) helps account for entertainment’s appeal. By identifying what unites disparate research traditions, this approach enables researchers across subfields to position their investigations within a shared theoretical landscape capable of generating cumulative, interconnected knowledge.

title: Deindividuation Among Gendered Violence Survivors and Posting About #MeToo
authors: Shannon Pappas, Kathryn D. Coduto, Jennifer Anderson
abstract: Abstract: Individuals have numerous channels to choose from when posting online, particularly when posting about sensitive or highly personal topics. This study uses the social identity model of deindividuation effects to examine why individuals posted about the #MeToo movement, considering whether they posted about their own experiences as survivors of gendered violence. Specifically, this manuscript offers an alternative theoretical perspective by focusing on positive deindividuation consequences. Participants ( N = 256) completed a survey measuring social identification and perceived anonymity affordances; participants also completed a perceived deindividuation scale that was created for this study and found to be reliable. Results reveal that survivors who posted with #MeToo had stronger group identification with others posting, higher perceptions of anonymity afforded on social network sites, and higher perceptions of deindividuation during #MeToo compared to survivors who chose not to post. This work offers theoretical implications related to positive deindividuating effects, as well as an exploratory measure for deindividuation experiences. Furthermore, this work discusses practical implications related to what makes an online social movement “successful.”

title: Explaining Science Knowledge Gaps on Social Media: Basic Science Knowledge and Intentional Versus Incidental Exposure
authors: Wenbo Li, Christine Gilbert, Shan Xu
abstract: This study examined whether basic science knowledge helps explain education-based gaps in domain-specific science knowledge and whether intentional and incidental exposure on social media condition those gaps. A national survey of American adults focused on two domains: climate change and algorithms. Results showed that basic science knowledge mediated the relationship between education and domain-specific knowledge across both domains. These indirect relationship were attenuated at higher levels of intentional social media exposure. The findings suggest that strengthening foundational science literacy and encouraging more deliberate engagement with science content on social media may help reduce knowledge disparities.

title: Work-Related Harassment and Intimidation in Journalism: Testing Identity-, Visibility-, and Influence-Based Explanations
authors: Ilmari Hiltunen, Ilari Törönen, Aleksi Suuronen, Reeta Pöyhtäri
abstract: Prior research shows that exposure to occupation-related harassment and intimidation varies considerably across journalists. This study tests three explanatory frameworks for this variation: identity-based explanations attributing heightened exposure to social hierarchies; visibility- and celebrity-capital-based explanations linking it to journalists’ varying levels of personal visibility and recognizability; and influence-based explanations attributing differences to the nature of journalistic work and its societal influence. Logistic regression analyses of survey data from Finnish journalists ( n = 932), examining verbal, legal, and physical forms of harassment and intimidation, lend strong support to influence-based explanations, partial support to visibility-based explanations, and limited support to identity-based explanations.

title: mlstats : An R Package for Multilevel Descriptive Statistics and Data Preparation
authors: Felix Dietrich
abstract: Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats , an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics—including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations—in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on Comprehensive R Archive Network with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/ .

title: Feelings among friends and foes in populist communication: The Finns Party leadership’s emotional appeals on social media during the 2023 Finnish parliamentary election
authors: Jesper Eklund, Jon Järviniemi
abstract: This study examines the use of emotional appeals in the social media communication by members of the populist radical right Finns Party leadership during the 2023 Finnish parliamentary election campaign. While previous research has highlighted the importance of emotions in populist communication, less empirical attention has been devoted to how populist radical right actors employ both negative and positive emotional appeals, how these appeals are directed toward different targets, and how their use varies across social media platforms. To address these gaps, we conducted a quantitative content analysis of 524 social media posts published on X (Twitter), TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram by six members of the Finns Party leadership. The findings show that negative emotional appeals are more prevalent and are primarily directed toward “elites” and “dangerous outgroups”, reinforcing a negative collective identity construction of antagonistic “others”. In contrast, positive emotional appeals are also used extensively and are primarily directed toward “the people” and populist actors as their representatives, reinforcing a positive collective identity construction of “us”. Finally, the analysis reveals variation across platforms, highlighting the need for further research on the relationship between social media platforms and emotional appeals.

title: Vaccine framing dynamics: Media influence, social media sharing, and public sensemaking during a crisis
authors: Austin Y. Hubner
abstract: During crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, information dissemination and sensemaking processes profoundly shape public perceptions. This study investigates the intricate interplay between media framing, social media sharing, and individual reinterpretation of COVID-19 vaccination news on Facebook. Analyzing 1957 articles from The New York Times (NYT) over 2 years, the research delves into news framing dynamics and their influence on Facebook sharing patterns. Findings reveal eight frames used by journalists, with a focus on scientific development, political controversy, and societal impact. Notably, the anti-vaccination frame received the highest number of shares per article. I also explored the content of the individual shares examining how individuals changed the information provided by the NYT during the sharing process.

title: Identifying Alternatives to Retraction of Controversial Research Findings
authors: Mitch Brown, Donald F. Sacco, August Namuth, Cory J. Clark, Nathan Honeycutt
abstract: Although academic journals have historically prioritized dissemination of accurate information, some journals now consider information hazards in editorial policies. Editors may reject or retract papers based on their perceived potential to impose societal harms. Such editorial policies have received pushback from scholars seeing such policies as impediments to effective science communication. Across four experiments, we tested how both scientists and everyday people view harm-based retractions and alternatives to retraction for addressing controversy. Academic researchers and lay perceivers disapproved of retractions based on information hazards, preferring commentaries, replications, adversarial collaborations, and even inaction . We offer policy recommendations for science communication.

title: Wise Empathy Improves Well-Being on Instagram
authors: Gregory John Depow, Christopher Oveis, Emily Zohar, Michael Inzlicht
abstract: Two-thirds of the global population spends significant time browsing social media, making it critical to understand how to improve online experiences to support well-being. Social media use is often linked to both positive and negative psychological outcomes, but interventions to enhance well-being during social media use remain limited. Here, we test whether an intervention embedded in daily life that trains individuals to use wise empathy on Instagram can improve users’ well-being. Drawing from strategic regulation of empathy and wisdom, we used an ecological momentary intervention to train half our sample ( N = 260) to wisely regulate empathy for positive and negative emotions on their own Instagram feeds. Using experience sampling ( N obs . = 5,902), we tracked empathy and well-being in daily life. The intervention increased wise empathy online – boosting appreciative joy, positive emotion sharing and compassion for negative emotions – while reducing negative emotion sharing, upward social comparisons and personal distress. On surveys where participants had recently browsed Instagram, those in the wise empathy condition reported higher well-being than controls, an effect mediated by changes in wise empathy. These findings position wise empathy as a scalable, trainable skill that can enhance well-being on social media by helping users engage more adaptively with emotional content. This work extends our understanding of how empathy predicts well-being and elucidates the relationship between social media use and well-being, with broad societal implications for our increasingly digital society.

title: When Movement Widens the Gap: The Contingent Effect of the Chinese #MeToo Movement on Feminist Attitudes
authors: Shuning Lu, Haixin Mu, Tian Yang
abstract: Social movements are often associated with various cultural outcomes, including shifts in public opinion regarding movement-related attitudes and ideologies. This study examines the shift of feminist attitudes among the public following the Chinese #MeToo movement. We develop a sociotechnical contingency framework that emphasizes how identity-based movement relevance and access to information channels shape the shifts in public opinion following social movements. Using nationally representative data from the Chinese General Social Survey (2010–2023), we find that the #MeToo movement was significantly associated with an increase in pro-feminist attitudes. These changes were unevenly distributed across groups, revealing widening attitudinal gaps along gender identities and digital divides. Our findings contribute to a nuanced understanding of how contemporary digitally mediated movements catalyze cultural change and underscore the need to contextualize their impact as it interacts with structural dynamics.

title: Do voting advice applications have durable causal effects? Evidence from concurrent survey and field experiments
authors: Micha Germann, Iulia Cioroianu, Fernando Mendez, Constantinos Djouvas
abstract: Voting advice applications (VAAs) are used by millions of voters, yet their causal effects on political knowledge, preferences, and behavior remain unclear. We present new evidence from two experiments conducted during the 2024 UK General Election: (1) a panel survey experiment that provides access to participants’ VAA advice, achieves high compliance with treatment assignment, and allows us to track outcomes over time; and (2) a concurrent field experiment embedded in a real-world VAA that allows us to assess the ecological validity of our findings. We find that VAA usage leads to durable changes in voters’ perception of how close they are to parties on policy issues, shifts party preferences in line with the advice received, and affects the vote choices of undecided voters. These results suggest that VAAs play an important role in election campaigns. However, we find no evidence that VAAs increase electoral participation.

title: Conditional Optimal Sampling: Enhancing Unequal-Probability Designs with Auxiliary Information
authors: P García-Segador, P Miranda
abstract: We address the problem of selecting a fixed-size sample from a finite population when the goal is to reduce the estimation error as much as possible. Our approach builds on the idea of choosing samples that are nearly optimal with respect to the values of the study variable, even though these values are not observed in advance. Instead, we rely on predictions derived from auxiliary information, for example, through statistical or machine-learning models, and construct sampling designs that are optimal for these predicted values. We show that this strategy is remarkably effective: even when the predictions are imperfect, the resulting designs tend to be very close to the unknown optimal design based on the true values. To understand why this happens, we study the geometric structure underlying the space of all feasible sampling designs and use this perspective to develop practical algorithms. Simulation experiments indicate that the proposed methodology achieves noticeably lower estimation error than classical unequal-probability sampling methods commonly used in the literature, including balanced procedures such as cube and classical fixed-size designs like conditional Poisson sampling.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Motivating The Unmotivated? Testing Conditional Lottery Incentives in an Ongoing Panel Survey
authors: Rasmus Patton, Jannes Jacobsen, Jörg Dollmann, Almuth Lietz
abstract: This study examines whether conditional lottery incentives, where the probability of winning increases with continued participation, can motivate panelists to reengage in a randomly sampled, quarterly online survey. Respondents were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a control group (CG) receiving the standard €10 incentive, treatment group 1 (T1) with an additional lottery offering ten Amazon vouchers worth €500, and treatment group 2 (T2) introducing conditionality by linking the probability of winning to participation in successive waves. This design tests whether reengagement depends not only on incentive size but also on respondents’ perceived ability to influence their odds of winning. Results show no statistically significant treatment effects. Neither the high-value lottery nor its conditional variant increased participation. Subgroup analyses reveal no systematic differences across prior participation, education, income, or country of origin. These findings confirm earlier evidence on the limited effectiveness of lotteries in survey research but extend it by testing conditionality as a motivational mechanism. Although conditional incentives strengthen the conceptual link between effort and reward, restoring agency alone appears insufficient to overcome deeper motivational barriers in quarterly online panels.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Using Recordings of Survey Interviews and Machine Learning to Evaluate Differences in Interviewer–Respondent Interactions Between Telephone, In-Person, and Video Interviews
authors: Hanyu Sun, Brad Edwards, Ting Yan
abstract: Computer-Assisted Recorded Interviewing captures audio recordings of survey interviews in real time, producing a distinctive form of unstructured paradata—question-level audio files that capture the question–answer sequences between the interviewer and respondent. These recordings offer insights into the survey response process, enabling a deeper understanding of how responses are formed and delivered. This paper explores the use of machine learning to automate the processing of recordings and to compare interviewer–respondent interactions in video interviews with those of in-person and telephone interviews in the production environment of a large national survey of US households. We first applied machine learning algorithms to transcribe the audio recordings and generate indicators describing interviewer–respondent interactions. We then assessed differences across the three modes in two interviewer behaviors indicative of adherence to standardized interviewing protocol (reading questions verbatim and maintaining question meaning) and in three interaction outcome measures indicative of respondent difficulty answering survey questions (number of the respondent’s turns, duration of the respondent’s first turn, and the total duration of turns with speech). We found significant differences in interviewer question reading behaviors and in the duration of the respondent’s first turn across the three modes, but the differences were small. Additionally, the question itself emerged as the primary source of variability across all outcome measures. This paper demonstrates a viable method for using recordings to efficiently assess interviewer–respondent interactions for research purposes.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Addressing Missing Data From Prompt Noncompliance: A Practical Guide to Auxiliary Variables in Ecological Momentary Assessment
authors: Stefan Schneider, Marta Walentynowicz, Meynard J. Toledo, Raymond Hernandez, Doerte U. Junghaenel, Joshua M. Smyth, Arthur A. Stone
abstract: Missing data from noncompliance and missed prompts are pervasive in ecological-momentary-assessment (EMA) research. Although researchers often examine variables associated with prompt nonresponse, these variables are rarely incorporated into analytic models, leaving standard multilevel analyses to rely on missing-at-random (MAR) assumptions that are often implausible given the available data. In this tutorial, we introduce an accessible strategy for integrating such variables, known as “auxiliary variables,” directly into multilevel models to bolster the plausibility of the MAR assumption. We outline a practical framework for identifying promising auxiliary variables in EMA data sets (e.g., structural-design features, lagged self-reports, passive metadata) and provide step-by-step instructions for (a) preparing EMA data sets, (b) evaluating the utility of candidate auxiliary variables, and (c) incorporating them into multilevel models of EMA data. To facilitate adoption, we supply open-source R code for each step and introduce an R function ( EMAuxiliary ) that streamlines the estimation of multilevel models with auxiliary variables using freely available Blimp software. A fully worked example using real EMA data illustrates the approach. Our aim is to equip applied researchers with a practical, widely applicable method for reducing bias from missing prompts and strengthening inferences in EMA studies.
journal_full: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

title: Classifying strategy use in multiattribute subjective choice: Application to conjoint experiments in political science
authors: Nidhi V. Banavar, Kirk Bansak
abstract: Conjoint experiments are extensively used across multiple disciplines to make inferences about preferences over multiattribute alternatives. Much previous research has analyzed the importance of attributes at the aggregate level. Here, we focus on understanding individual-level behavior and, specifically, on strategy use. We present a Bayesian cognitive model of strategy use that performs attribute weight inference (how important an attribute is), attribute level inference (which value of the attribute is favored), and latent-mixture inference to classify strategy use among well-established strategies in cognitive science. We then validate and apply our model to two conjoint experiments ( N = 3,762) focusing on three political domains (attitudes toward immigrants, political candidates, and climate policy). We find that the simplest heuristic strategy is the highest probability in all conditions and that approximately 67–76% of subjects are classified as using different strategies depending on the political domain. Our model additionally highlights how aggregate-level inference on the weight of an attribute can be meaningfully decomposed by individual differences in strategy use and preferences over attributes. In addition, our experiments include a set of experimental design manipulations that increase different dimensions of complexity and show their impact on strategy classification.
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
